record.description: Hildebrandt's central thesis. Against the scholarly consensus (Long, Sharples, Frede, Hahmann) that all of Alexander's objections in De fato fail, she argues that one succeeds: an innovative version of the Lazy Argument at De fato XXI (191,2-25). It does not claim, as traditional versions do, that actions do not matter; it claims that, since the truth of Stoic determinism is uncertain, it is too risky to believe it, because the belief can give average rational agents good reasons to be lazy. Safer therefore not to believe it.
record.label: Hildebrandt: Alexander's new Lazy Argument is a risk/safety argument against Stoic determinism

record.description: Hildebrandt agrees with Long, Sharples, Frede and Hahmann that many of Alexander's De fato objections (e.g. the appeal to contingent properties to endechomenon, IX 174,30-175,7, and to chance effects apo tuches, 171,18-175,28) miss their target. Alexander is misled by, or knowingly exploits, the homonymy of 'contingent': he uses it in the Aristotelian sense 'not determined by the subject's essence' / 'has only accidental causes', whereas the Stoics use it in the sense 'not determined by past and present causal factors'. A property can be contingent in the Aristotelian sense and necessary in the Stoic sense, so the objection is not a genuine counterexample.
record.label: Hildebrandt: most Alexandrian objections fail by exploiting the homonymy of 'contingent'

record.description: Hildebrandt's key reconstructive move: Alexander's argument need not show that the perfect rational agent (the Stoic sage) would become lazy, only that the average rational agent could, given limited epistemic access. So the Stoics need not be wrong about determinism; their views need only be controversial. Beyond Alexander's own reason (that one might conclude actions do not matter), Hildebrandt adds two further reasons drawn partly from Brennan (2005): (1) doubt about whether deliberations/actions are up to us, since individual nature is not ultimately up to us; (2) doubt, following Brennan, that one cannot know which action is co-fated with the desired outcome, making laziness rational.
record.label: Hildebrandt: the argument targets the average, not the perfect, rational agent

record.description: To strengthen the Stoic reply to the worry that necessitated acts are not 'up to us' (eph' hemin), Hildebrandt adduces Chrysippus' cylinder analogy (Cicero, De fato 42-43; Gellius, NA VII.2, 11-13). Two causal factors are distinguished: (a) the external impetus (preceding cause) and (b) the agent's individual nature/character (complete cause, via assent to an impression). Actions are up to us not because we could have chosen otherwise, but because they are determined primarily by factors internal to us and free from external coercion; this makes us morally responsible and answers the worry an Aristotelian like Alexander could raise.
record.label: Hildebrandt: Chrysippus' rolling-cylinder analogy grounds moral responsibility under determinism

record.description: Exposition of Alexander's new Lazy Argument (De fato XXI, 191,2-25). Alexander compares two errors under uncertainty: (i) determinism is true but we believe it false, and (ii) determinism is false but we believe it true. Error (i) costs little: if all is fated, those who believe they have power err only in words, not deeds (191,13-17), because they were not in control anyway. Error (ii) is dangerous: believing determinism true can make agents lazy and abandon good but strenuous deeds (191,17-23). Hence one should choose the less dangerous road. Hildebrandt notes Weidemann (1999) likens this to (half of) Pascal's Wager.
record.label: Hildebrandt: De fato XXI weighs the asymmetric risk of believing vs. disbelieving determinism

record.description: Hildebrandt extends Alexander's argument beyond what he states: the risk of making average agents lazy arises not only if Stoic determinism is false but also if it is true. If determinism is true and agents correctly believe it, the same reasons can still persuade them that laziness is permissible, and they may refrain from good but strenuous deeds that the Stoics would deem impermissible. Their laziness would be predetermined, yet it would still have been better had they not believed determinism. In either case, promoting belief in Stoic determinism on a large scale is dangerous for average rational agents; no Stoic response to this new version has been transmitted.
record.label: Hildebrandt: the laziness risk obtains even if Stoic determinism is true

record.description: Hildebrandt distinguishes Alexander's three Lazy-Argument versions. The first (De fato XI, 179,12-20) claims that under determinism deliberation is useless, since after deliberating one must do what one would have done without deliberating; the second (XVI, 186,30-187,2) claims that effort is useless, so people would choose easy over noble actions. Both give the core Ciceronian Lazy Argument (Cicero, De fato 28-29) Alexander's own spin but remain unconvincing.
record.label: Hildebrandt: Alexander's first two Lazy Arguments (uselessness of deliberation / of effort) are unconvincing

record.description: Article in Studia Philosophica Estonica 15 (2022): 25-44. Argues that, although most of Alexander of Aphrodisias' objections to Stoic determinism in De fato are unconvincing, one argument is more successful: an innovative version of the Lazy Argument (argos logos, De fato XXI). Unlike traditional versions, it does not claim that actions do not matter, but that it is too risky to believe Stoic determinism because, given uncertainty, the belief can give average rational agents good reasons to be lazy.
record.label: Hildebrandt 2022 — Alexander of Aphrodisias' Lazy Arguments against Stoic Determinism
